opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's trickier than it looks, because the two families optimize different things and you can easily end up comparing apples to oranges.

The first thing I'd say is that you want to hold the obvious variables fixed: same data, same tokenizer, roughly the same parameter count, and ideally the same training compute. A lot of early comparisons were unfair in one direction or another. Autoregressive models have had years of engineering and recipe tuning behind them, so if you train a diffusion model with a recipe that was really designed for next-token prediction, you're probably handicapping it. Conversely, you can make diffusion look great by giving it more compute or a better data mix. So controlling the training budget matters a lot.

Then there's the question of what you measure. For autoregressive models, perplexity is the natural metric because you get exact likelihoods. Diffusion models typically give you a bound on the likelihood, so if you compare a bound against an exact value you're already slightly penalizing diffusion. That's fine, it's conservative, but you have to be aware of it. And perplexity alone isn't the whole story. Ultimately people care about downstream quality: does the model answer questions correctly, does it write good code, does it follow instructions.

The other piece I think is really important is inference. The big promise of diffusion for language is that you aren't locked into generating one token at a time, left to right. You can generate many tokens in parallel and refine them, so there's a quality-versus-speed tradeoff you can actually control by choosing the number of denoising steps. So the fair way to compare is not just "which model is better," but "for a given latency or a given amount of inference compute, what quality do you get?" You want to draw that whole frontier. If you only look at one point, say the autoregressive model at full quality versus diffusion at some arbitrary step count, you miss the real story, which is that diffusion can often give you comparable quality much faster on modern hardware, because it uses the GPU more efficiently than sequential decoding.

And finally, you should test the things each paradigm is naturally good or bad at. Diffusion models can do infilling, editing, and controllable generation quite naturally, and they don't suffer from some of the left-to-right issues, like the so-called reversal curse. Autoregressive models have a very mature ecosystem around things like KV caching and long-context serving. A fair evaluation should look at both the standard benchmarks and these capability differences, so you get an honest picture rather than one leaderboard number.

r001.rationale: The response recommends controlling data, parameter count, and compute, but does not claim that any remaining performance differences are attributable entirely to the modeling paradigm.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and honestly it's something we've thought about a lot, because it's very easy to do an unfair comparison in either direction.

The first thing I'd say is that you have to control for the obvious confounders. Same architecture, or as close as you can get, same parameter count, same training data, same number of tokens seen, same compute budget. A lot of the early results people pointed to, where diffusion looked worse, were really comparing a diffusion model trained from scratch on a modest budget against an autoregressive model that had benefited from years of engineering and scaling. That's not a comparison of the paradigms, that's a comparison of maturity.

The second thing is that you have to be careful about what you're measuring. Autoregressive models give you an exact likelihood, so perplexity is the natural metric. Diffusion models give you a bound on the likelihood, and that bound can be loose. So if you just compare perplexity numbers, you're penalizing the diffusion model for something that may not actually reflect sample quality or downstream performance. We've found it's much more informative to look at downstream tasks, generation quality, and things like controllability, infilling, or how the model behaves when you let it reason over the whole sequence at once.

And then the third dimension, which I think is actually the most interesting one, is inference. These models have very different cost profiles. An autoregressive model is bound by the number of tokens, one forward pass per token, essentially. A diffusion model is bound by the number of denoising steps, and that number is something you get to choose. So you can trade off quality and latency in a way that autoregressive models fundamentally can't. If you only compare at a fixed quality and ignore speed, or only compare at a fixed speed and ignore quality, you're missing half the story. The right picture is a frontier, quality versus cost, and asking where each approach sits on that curve.

So I'd summarize it as: match the training conditions, use metrics that don't structurally favor one side, and compare at the level of the whole quality-versus-compute tradeoff rather than a single point. When you do that, I think the diffusion story looks a lot more compelling than people initially assumed.

r001.rationale: The response recommends matching architecture, parameter count, and training data, but does not say that any remaining performance difference is entirely attributable to the modeling paradigm. It also emphasizes other factors, including training maturity, evaluation metrics, and inference cost.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is, what are you holding fixed? You want to control for things like the training data, the model size, and the amount of compute used for training. If you compare a diffusion model with an auto-regressive model that has had much more training or much more engineering effort behind it, it’s hard to isolate the effect of the modeling approach itself.

But there’s also the inference side, and that’s where the comparison gets interesting. An auto-regressive model generates tokens sequentially, whereas a diffusion model can update many tokens in parallel, but it may need multiple rounds of refinement. So the number of generation steps alone doesn’t tell you which one is faster or cheaper. You have to measure latency and compute on comparable hardware, at a comparable level of output quality.

I would really want to see a quality-versus-compute curve, rather than just one number. How good are the outputs when you give each model a particular inference budget? And how does that change with sequence length or with the task? That gives us a much better picture of where each approach has an advantage.

r001.rationale: The response recommends controlling for training data and model size, and says this helps isolate the modeling approach’s effect. It does not state that architecture is held constant or that performance differences are attributable entirely to the modeling paradigm.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is, what are you holding fixed? You can compare models with the same number of parameters, trained on the same data, but that doesn’t necessarily mean they use the same amount of compute, either during training or at inference time.

With an autoregressive model, you generate one token at a time. With a diffusion model, you can update many tokens in parallel, but you might need multiple rounds of refinement. So counting the number of generation steps alone isn’t a fair comparison either. You really want to look at the quality you get for a given computational budget, and then also measure latency on the hardware you care about, because parallelism can make a big difference.

And I would be careful about drawing conclusions from a single operating point. There’s a tradeoff between speed and quality. Ideally, you would compare those curves across different budgets, with comparable data and training resources. That gives you a much better picture of where each approach is useful.

r001.rationale: The response discusses matching parameter count and training data, but explicitly says compute can still differ and recommends comparing quality across computational budgets. It does not attribute performance differences entirely to the modeling paradigm with architecture, parameter count, and data held constant.
